background.definition: Lipomas are adipose tumors commonly located in the subcutaneous tissues of the head, neck, shoulders, and back, but they may be found in any subcutaneous location.

list.listitem: 1 per 1000 persons per year.
80% of all lipomas are solitary.
Most lipomas present between the ages of 40 and 60 years.
Multiple lipomas are more common in young men.
Solitary lipomas have been associated with rearrangements of chromosome 12, but the data are not definitive.
There may be an association with trauma, but there is uncertainty as to whether the trauma was causative or led to discovery.
Lipomas are slowly growing nodules composed of mature adipocytes arranged in lobules, often surrounded by a fibrous capsule.
Occasionally, nonencapsulated lipomas will infiltrate into surrounding muscle and nerves.
They are painless in nature, unless they have infiltrated surrounding structures.
There are four histologic variations of benign lipomas (see ).
80% are less than 5 cm in diameter, but they can reach 20 cm.
Clinical findings are sufficient to make the diagnosis of lipoma. C
A fixed or painful or rapidly growing mass, or one with apparent invasion into local tissues are concerning symptoms for malignant disease. C
MRI is the imaging modality of choice when malignancy is suspected. C
Multiple lipomas may indicate the presence of a syndrome. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Communicates to the skin through a small keratinized plug
Rapid growth, pain, and local invasion
Occurs after trauma and is typically quite firm and tender
Arises from the mesodermal and dermal cells; positive Fitzpatrick's sign, which is dimpling or retraction of the lesion beneath the skin with lateral compression

list.listitem: A slowly growing subcutaneous tumor on the upper trunk or head with a soft, doughy feel is most likely a lipoma. Palpation is quite specific but not sensitive, so it is more useful when positive for lipoma than for ruling it out when negative.
Patients often present with a history of trauma to the same area, or nearby, prompting concern that the trauma may have caused the lipoma.
Lipomas are also frequently discovered by chance during routine physical examinations.

Masses that are fixed, painful, rapidly growing or are accompanied by apparent invasion into local tissues are concerning symptoms for malignant disease, indicating the need for further investigation including biopsy and/or MRI.

Although the diagnosis is a clinical one, MRI can be used to differentiate a benign from a malignant lipoma when there are clinical features suspicious for malignancy such as painful, fixed, or rapidly growing mass.

A systematic review of 26 studies with 2613 patients found that the overall accuracy of radiologist gestalt (using CT and/or MRI) for distinguishing liposarcoma from benign lesions was 85% sensitive and 63% specific (LR+ 2.3, LR- 0.25).
Biopsy is used to make the definitive diagnosis of benign lipoma vs liposarcoma.

Ultrasound is also fairly accurate in the differentiation of lipoma from other soft tissue tumors. On ultrasound, superficial lipomas are discrete masses with fusiform edges that are isoechoic when compared to subcutaneous fat. Noninflamed epidermoid cysts, a common differential diagnosis for lipoma, are discrete round or ovoid masses with varying echogenicity compared to subcutaneous fat, and often demonstrate posterior acoutic enhancement.
MDM2 amplification is a mutation found in well-differentiated liposarcomas and has been proposed as a way to differentiate them from benign lipomas.
No relevant clinical decision rules are found.
The diagnosis of lipoma can be made reliably based on the clinical examination of a round, mobile, nontender subcutaneous lesion with a soft, doughy consistency.
Excision with biopsy should be considered for a fast growing lipoma, one that is painful, or one that appears to invade local tissue.
MRI can be used to distinguish benign from malignant lesions.
Treatment is not necessary unless there are cosmetic concerns, evidence of compression of neighboring structures, or an uncertain diagnosis. C
Surgical excision often results in a cure. C
Liposuction and steroid injections are less effective alternatives. C
Lipoma excision is most common, whether through a large incision, or via the minimal excision technique.
Begin by outlining the margins of the lipoma. This will aid in ensuring complete removal.
A field block with 1% to 2% lidocaine with epinephrine into the subcutaneous tissues usually provides sufficient anesthesia.
Large lipomas may require removal of a portion of skin, subcutaneous sutures to close the dead space, and superficial skin sutures as well.
Small lipomas may be squeezed through a 3- to 4-mm incision; often no sutures are required.

The MOTIF (Minimal One-Third Incision and Four-Step) approach makes an incision 1/3 the length of the long axis of the lipoma, dissects superficially, then circumferentially, then extracts the lipoma and cuts the stalk.
Unless the lipoma appears unusual, pathology evaluation is unnecessary.

Liposuction with a large syringe and large-bore needle (16 gauge) may be implemented in areas where a scar is unwanted, although complete elimination of the lipoma is difficult with this technique. A small amount of dilute lidocaine is sufficient anesthesia.

Fat atrophy is a known side effect of steroid injection, which has been tried with lipomas less than 1 inch in diameter. A 1:1 mixture of lidocaine and Kenalog for a total of 1 to 3 mL is commonly attempted. Injections may be repeated monthly.
Lipomas are benign subcutaneous tumors that are rarely malignant. C
Recurrence of lipomas is uncommon. C

feature.caption: Histological Variants of Lipoma.
feature.feature_body:
Histologic Type Microscopic Findings
Angiolipoma Coexisting vascular proliferation; may be painful and usually arise shortly after puberty
Pleomorphic Bizarre, multinucleated giant cells are admixed with normal adipocytes; occur predominantly in men 50-70 years of age
Spindle cell Slender spindle cells are admixed in a localized area of normal-appearing adipocytes
Adenolipoma Newly described superficial lipoma with eccrine sweat glands; often located on the proximal upper extremities
Data from Salam GA. Lipoma excision. Am Fam Physician 2002;65:901-904.
